items.title: Pakistan rejects Afghan Taliban's claims of civilian casualties in counterterrorism operations
items.description: The Foreign Office (FO) on Monday rejected allegations made by the Afghan Taliban government regarding civilian casualties in Islamabad’s counterterrorism campaign in the neighbouring country, maintaining that Pakistan’s conduct always “reflected restraint” and the response was “proportionate to the level of threat”. The Afghan Taliban have repeatedly claimed civilian casualties in Pakistani strikes in Afghanistan; Pakistani authorities have denied the accusations, holding that they target military and terrorist infrastructure. Recently, a spokesperson for the Afghan Ministry of Foreign Affairs claimed in an interview with CNN that 1,119 Afghan civilians were killed or injured in Pakistani military strikes in Afghanistan since late 2021, according to Afghan media. In a statement issued on Monday, the FO rejected the “baseless and unsubstantiated” allegations regarding civilian casualties attributed to Pakistan’s counterterrorism operations. “Disinformation and misleading narratives will neither obscure the threat posed by the terrorist networks operating from Afghan territory nor absolve the Afghan Taliban regime of its responsibility to prevent Afghan soil from being used to plan and launch attacks against Pakistan,” the FO said, adding that attacks emanating from Afghan soil had claimed more than 3,500 casualties in 2026. It further said that various relevant United Nations mechanisms had reported the situation as well, and the issue had been raised as a serious concern for the international community. The FO noted that the Afghan Taliban continued to “shelter with impunity a large number of terrorist organisations, including the Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), the Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA) and their affiliates, which continue to pose a serious threat to the peace and stability of the region and beyond”. It said that thousands of Pakistani civilians had been martyred in terrorist attacks, which it said were “planned, financed, supported and carried out” from Afghan soil under the “watch, patronage and active facilitation” of the Afghan Taliban. “No responsible state can remain passive when its civilians and security forces are repeatedly targeted,” the statement read. It maintained that Pakistan’s actions in response to terrorist attacks had been undertaken in exercise of self-defence, according to the principles of necessity and as a last resort. The FO further stated that the actions were “directed only and exclusively against terrorists and their logistical support bases in Afghanistan”. The statement stressed that Pakistan’s response had been “proportionate to the level of threat” and adhered to the principles of “distinction and precaution”. “The scale and scope of the action reflected restraint, particularly in light of the severity and frequency of terrorist attacks faced by Pakistan. Pakistan rejects any insinuations otherwise,” it said. The FO called on the international community to hold the Afghan Taliban regime accountable for “failure to uphold obligations” under various international commitments. “Pakistan reserves the right to take all necessary measures in order to safeguard its sovereignty, territorial integrity, and the safety and security of Pakistani nationals,” it said. According to a UN Security Council-mandated monitoring report — covering the period from Dec 16, 2025 to June 9, 2026 — the Afg­han Taliban’s continued support for TTP has contributed to a rise in the frequency and lethality of terrorist attacks in Pakistan, even as Kabul has taken some initial steps to rein in the group. Ties between Pakistan and Afghanistan have been strained in the past few years as Islamabad continues to voice its concern over cross-border terrorism. Islamabad has repeatedly urged the Taliban administration in Kabul to dismantle terrorist sanctuaries on Afghan soil, particularly those linked to the banned TTP, that are used for attacks in Pakistan. Officials say those appeals have gone unheeded. September witnessed another bout of conflict between the two neighbours, with Pakistan carrying out calibrated airstrikes in the border region in response to terrorist attacks in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. This was followed by drone incursions from across the border, which Islamabad said were shot down, and two further rounds of retaliatory airstrikes. Over the weekend, the information ministry rejected former United States envoy Zalmay Khalilzad’s “baseless and misleading allegations” that Pakistan was “arming Afghans to fight the Taliban”. It also rebutted the Afghan Taliban’s stance that it lacked the “capabilities” to fuel insecurity in other countries and criticised it for resorting to “diversionary allegations” instead of preventing the use of Afghanistan’s soil for terrorist attacks against Pakistan.

items.title: 10 millions de F CFA volés, le suspect trahi par les clés des bureaux
items.description: En Côte d’Ivoire, un homme de 36 ans a été interpellé à Bouaké après le vol de 10 millions de F CFA dans les bureaux d’une société de vente d’engins à deux et trois roues. La totalité de la somme a été retrouvée au domicile du suspect, à l’issue d’une perquisition menée dans le cadre de l’opération Épervier spécial, selon la Police nationale ivoirienne, qui a rendu l’information publique dimanche 25 octobre 2026. Dix millions de F CFA dérobés, mais intégralement récupérés. À Bouaké, dans le centre de la Côte d’Ivoire, les investigations menées par les forces de police ont permis de retrouver la totalité d’une somme d’argent volée dans les locaux d’une entreprise située au quartier Nimbo. Tout est parti d’une plainte déposée par le directeur de cette société spécialisée dans la vente d’engins à deux et trois roues. Saisis de l’affaire, les policiers du Commissariat du 4ᵉ Arrondissement ont mené des investigations dans le cadre de l’opération Épervier spécial. Le jeudi 22 octobre 2026, les recherches ont conduit les enquêteurs au domicile du principal suspect, au quartier Socopao. La perquisition effectuée sur place a permis de découvrir les 10 millions de F CFA, dissimulés dans un drap. Des clés copiées pour accéder aux bureaux Au cours de son audition, le mis en cause, identifié par les initiales N.G. et âgé de 36 ans, a reconnu les faits. Selon les éléments communiqués par la Police nationale ivoirienne, il a déclaré avoir fait reproduire les clés des bureaux de l’entreprise, ce qui lui permettait d’y entrer sans effraction. La totalité de la somme dérobée a été restituée au responsable de la société. Quant au suspect, il a été conduit au Parquet pour la suite de la procédure judiciaire. Cette affaire illustre l’issue des investigations engagées dans le cadre de l’opération Épervier spécial, avec la récupération intégrale des fonds et leur restitution à leur propriétaire. Le sort judiciaire du mis en cause reste désormais entre les mains de la justice. Par Valentin SOMANDE L’article 10 millions de F CFA volés, le suspect trahi par les clés des bureaux est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: Military clears air on troops’ clash with police personnel in Plateau
items.description: The Special Task Force Operation Enduring Peace (JTF-OPEP) has cleared the air on the recent encounter between its troops and personnel of the Nigeria Police Force (NPF) in Bassa Local Government Area (LGA) of Plateau. The media officer of the operation, Capt. Polycarp Oteh, in a statement on Monday in Jos, said that the encounter between the two security agencies was misconstrued to be a clash. The News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) reports that videos and photographs of an alleged clash between the military and police personnel went viral on social media a few days ago. It was alleged that troops had prevented the police personnel from going after some criminals in the area. But Oteh said that troops only responded to a distress call, following a sporadic shooting at Mai Farin Moto, Maraban Dere and adjoining communities of the area. “On Oct. 20, troops of our Sector 3 responded to a distress call reporting sporadic gunfire in Mai Farin Moto, Maraban Dere and adjoining communities. This is alongside reports of the suspected killing of a resident, Mr Adamu Suleiman. “The troops were deployed to the affected area to assess the security situation, establish the circumstances of the incident, prevent escalation and protect lives and property. “On arrival, the troops sought to engage the police personnel operating in the area to clarify the situation and facilitate a coordinated security response. “Regrettably, the interaction was characterised by a lack of cooperation from some personnel in spite of efforts to de-escalate tensions and maintain operational discipline,” he said. Oteh emphasised that troops’ intervention was prompted by an operational distress call, adding that it was undertaken in the interest of public safety. “JTF-OPEP remains committed to impartiality, professionalism and the protection of lives and property. “As a joint security arrangement, our operational effectiveness depends on inter-agency coordination, mutual respect, adherence to established procedures and unity of effort. “Issues arising from the incident are being addressed through appropriate command and inter-agency channels to establish the facts, sustain operational cohesion and prevent recurrence,” he explained. The media officer advised members of the public and reporters to verify information before going to the press, adding that such move would ensure credibility and professionalism. He assured residents of Plateau of its resolve to maintain law and order, protect innocent residents and consolidate peace and security across its joint operations area. (NAN) The post Military clears air on troops’ clash with police personnel in Plateau appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: La Bourse de Casablanca ouvre en hausse
items.description: La Bourse de Casablanca a démarré en hausse lundi, son indice phare, le MASI, gagnant 0,59% à 17.154,15 points (pts). Le MASI 20, qui regroupe les 20 valeurs les plus liquides, prenait 0,58% à 1.249,2 pts et le MASI ESG, indice des entreprises ayant la meilleure notation ESG selon Moody's ESG Solutions, se bonifiait de 1,09% à 1.263,53 pts. Le MASI Mid and Small Cap, reflétant la performance des petites et moyennes entreprises cotées, s'adjugeait, quant à lui, 0,6% à 1.642,53 pts. Aux valeurs individuelles, Jet Contractors (+5,07% à 1.575 DH), Taqa Morocco (+3,93% à 1.694 DH), Ciments du Maroc (+3,35% à 1.449 DH), Vicenne (+3,33% à 310 DH) et IB Maroc.com (+3% à 51,5 DH) réalisaient les meilleures performances. À l'inverse, Cartier Saada (-4,09% à 18,51 DH), CIH (-4,07% à 305,05 DH), Zellidja S.A (-3,89% à 221,05 DH), Med Paper (-3,81% à 21,45 DH) et Afriquia Gaz (-2,33% à 3.601 DH) accusaient les plus fortes baisses. Vendredi, le MASI avait clôturé sur une perte de 0,47%. The post La Bourse de Casablanca ouvre en hausse appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: À Madagascar, le processus de concertation nationale accumule les retards
items.description: À Madagascar, la concertation nationale n’a toujours pas débuté contrairement à ce que prévoyait le calendrier officiel publié en août par le Conseil œcuménique des Églises chrétiennes (FFKM), chargé de piloter le processus. L’organisation fait savoir que des facilitateurs sont en passe d’être déployés sur le terrain pour encadrer les consultations, sans pour autant confirmer la moindre date effective de démarrage. items.title: Budget 2026 : les dépenses portées à 3 993,3 milliards de FCFA
items.description: © Internet Le Conseil national de Transition a adopté jeudi le projet de loi de finances rectificative avec 121 voix favorables. Les dépenses augmentent de 415,1 milliards de FCFA et le déficit prévisionnel progresse de 100 milliards. Le Conseil national de Transition a adopté, jeudi 22 octobre, le projet de loi modifiant le budget de l’État pour 2026. Le texte avait été approuvé en Conseil des ministres le 3 juillet avant sa transmission à l’organe législatif. Les dépenses budgétaires passent de 3 578,217 milliards à 3 993,319 milliards de FCFA. Cette augmentation de 415,103 milliards représente une progression de 11,6 %. Les recettes sont relevées de 3 057,792 milliards à 3 372,895 milliards de FCFA. Leur hausse atteint 315,103 milliards, soit 10,3 %. La différence entre les recettes et les dépenses porte le déficit prévisionnel à 620,425 milliards de FCFA, contre 520,425 milliards dans le budget initial. Trois nouvelles sources de recettes Le projet de loi attribue 100 milliards de FCFA de recettes supplémentaires à l’amélioration du produit de la taxe ad valorem appliquée au secteur minier. Cette progression est liée à l’évolution du cours de l’or, selon la note de présentation du ministère de l’Économie et des Finances. La taxe sur les gains des paris sportifs doit apporter 50 milliards de FCFA. Les contributions destinées aux fonds miniers représentent 165,103 milliards supplémentaires. Quatre comptes spéciaux du Trésor sont concernés. Le Fonds minier de développement local doit recevoir 18,436 milliards de FCFA. Le fonds consacré aux infrastructures énergétiques, hydrauliques et de transport représente 121,573 milliards. Le financement de la recherche géologique, de la formation et du renforcement des capacités atteint 24,475 milliards. Une enveloppe de 619 millions de FCFA est affectée à la promotion du secteur minier. Du côté des dépenses, le texte inscrit 200 milliards de FCFA de crédits de paiement supplémentaires pour les opérations de sécurisation du territoire. Il prévoit également une subvention exceptionnelle de 50 milliards de FCFA à la Compagnie malienne pour le développement des textiles. Un prêt de 30 milliards de FCFA à la CMDT figure parmi les charges de trésorerie. Quinze établissements sanitaires concernés Le programme sanitaire présenté devant le CNT prévoit la transformation des centres de santé de référence des six communes de Bamako en hôpitaux de district modernes. Deux hôpitaux de district doivent être construits à Kangaba et à Bla. Sept hôpitaux régionaux sont également annoncés à Koulikoro, San, Koutiala, Bougouni, Dioïla, Nioro et Bandiagara. Ces quinze opérations seront financées sur le budget national, selon le compte rendu de la séance. Le montant affecté séparément à chaque établissement et le calendrier des travaux n’ont pas été communiqués. La Commission des finances du CNT a par ailleurs demandé au gouvernement de l’informer de toute ouverture de crédits par décret d’avance. Elle recommande également la publication périodique des ressources obtenues grâce à la cession de bâtiments appartenant à l’État. Le vote du 22 octobre approuve ainsi la nouvelle enveloppe budgétaire et les changements de recettes et de dépenses. L’exécution des crédits consacrés aux hôpitaux, à la sécurité, à la CMDT et aux fonds miniers apparaîtra dans les prochains états d’exécution du budget.

items.title: Brésil : Lula démontre qu’aucun retard électoral n’est irréversible [Par Aboubacar Sakho]
items.description: Arrivé en deuxième position au premier tour, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva a réussi une remontée sans précédent dans l’histoire de la démocratie brésilienne depuis le rétablissement de l’élection présidentielle directe en 1989. Sa victoire face à Flávio Bolsonaro repose notamment sur une stratégie de mobilisation des abstentionnistes, une campagne numérique renforcée et une reconquête du terrain. Le Brésil vient de vivre un épisode majeur de son histoire politique. Le dimanche 25 octobre 2026, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva a remporté le second tour de l’élection présidentielle, battant Flávio Bolsonaro et obtenant un quatrième mandat présidentiel non consécutif. À la veille de son 81e anniversaire, qu’il célébrera le 27 octobre, le dirigeant brésilien offre une nouvelle démonstration de sa capacité à mobiliser une partie importante de l’électorat dans un pays profondément polarisé. Selon les résultats définitifs annoncés par le Tribunal supérieur électoral (TSE), Lula a recueilli 51,79 % des suffrages valablement exprimés, soit 64 256 232 voix, contre 48,21 % pour son adversaire, qui a obtenu 59 826 041 voix. L’écart, de plus de 4,4 millions de suffrages, confirme une victoire nette dans une élection pourtant très disputée. La portée historique de cette victoire tient d’abord au chemin parcouru entre les deux tours. Le 4 octobre, Flávio Bolsonaro avait terminé en tête du premier tour avec 47,03 % des suffrages, contre 45,16 % pour Lula. Le candidat du Parti des travailleurs abordait donc le second tour avec un retard de près de deux points, tandis que plusieurs enquêtes d’opinion donnaient un léger avantage à son adversaire. Lula a néanmoins réussi à inverser le rapport de forces. Selon les analyses publiées au lendemain du scrutin, c’est la première fois depuis le retour des élections présidentielles directes en 1989 qu’un candidat arrivé deuxième au premier tour remporte finalement le second. Cette performance ne s’explique pas par un seul facteur. Elle résulte d’une combinaison de mobilisation électorale, de stratégie de communication, de rassemblement politique et de capacité à convaincre des électeurs qui n’avaient pas choisi Lula au premier tour. L’un des principaux axes de la stratégie de Lula a consisté à s’adresser aux électeurs qui n’avaient pas participé au premier tour. Le 4 octobre, environ 33,4 millions d’électeurs étaient restés à l’écart du scrutin, portant le taux d’abstention à 21,08 %. Pour le camp de Lula, cette masse d’électeurs constituait un enjeu considérable. Dans une compétition aussi serrée, convaincre une partie des abstentionnistes de se déplacer pouvait modifier l’équilibre électoral. Il ne suffisait donc pas de consolider le vote traditionnel du Parti des travailleurs : il fallait aussi ramener aux urnes des citoyens désabusés, indécis ou peu convaincus par les candidats. La stratégie a été accompagnée d’une mobilisation de terrain et d’une campagne ciblant les électeurs susceptibles de changer d’avis. Le taux d’abstention est finalement descendu à environ 19,21 % au second tour, soit près de deux points de moins qu’au premier. Cette baisse ne signifie pas que tous les nouveaux votants ont choisi Lula. Elle témoigne toutefois d’une participation accrue, dans un scrutin où chaque déplacement électoral pouvait compter. Les enquêtes préélectorales indiquaient par ailleurs que Lula disposait d’un potentiel de soutien parmi certains abstentionnistes et les électeurs ayant voté blanc ou nul au premier tour. Lula a également renforcé sa présence sur les réseaux sociaux. Son équipe a privilégié des vidéos plus spontanées, notamment au format selfie, afin de s’adresser directement aux électeurs et de rendre sa communication moins institutionnelle. Parallèlement, des mouvements sociaux, des étudiants et des militants ont organisé des rassemblements dans de nombreuses villes. Cette mobilisation a permis de maintenir une présence visible sur le terrain et de donner une dynamique collective à la campagne du président sortant. L’association des réseaux numériques et des manifestations physiques a constitué l’un des ressorts importants de la remontée. Elle a permis de toucher des publics différents, de renforcer la participation militante et de relayer les messages de campagne au-delà des structures traditionnelles du parti. La campagne de Lula s’est également appuyée sur la continuité de ses politiques sociales, notamment en matière de lutte contre la pauvreté, de soutien aux ménages modestes et d’accès à l’éducation. Son bilan historique, marqué par des programmes tels que Bolsa Família, a contribué à entretenir son ancrage auprès des catégories populaires. Dans un pays où le coût de la vie, l’endettement des ménages et la sécurité publique occupent une place importante dans le débat politique, le candidat a cherché à convaincre que son projet pouvait répondre aux préoccupations quotidiennes de la population. Il a également bénéficié du soutien d’électeurs qui, sans nécessairement adhérer à l’ensemble de son programme, souhaitaient empêcher le retour au pouvoir de la famille Bolsonaro. Cette logique de rassemblement a dépassé le seul électorat traditionnel de la gauche et a contribué à élargir sa base au second tour. Il serait toutefois excessif d’attribuer sa victoire à un seul groupe d’électeurs ou à une mesure particulière. Le résultat final traduit plusieurs mouvements simultanés dans un pays où les préférences politiques restent fortement divisées. La portée de cette élection dépasse largement les frontières nationales. Avec une population représentant près de la moitié de celle de l’Amérique du Sud, le Brésil occupe une place centrale dans les équilibres politiques, économiques et diplomatiques du continent. Première économie sud-américaine, il joue un rôle déterminant dans les débats sur le commerce international, la transition énergétique, la protection de l’Amazonie, la coopération régionale et les relations avec les grandes puissances. La réélection de Lula signifie que le pays poursuivra, au moins dans ses grandes orientations, une politique de gauche et de centre gauche, axée notamment sur les programmes sociaux, la souveraineté nationale et la recherche de relations internationales diversifiées. Elle intervient également dans un contexte régional où plusieurs forces conservatrices ont enregistré des succès électoraux. Cette victoire ne garantit cependant pas à Lula une gouvernance facile. Le pays demeure profondément polarisé, et le président devra composer avec un Congrès où les forces conservatrices disposent d'une influence importante, ainsi qu'avec les attentes économiques et sociales d'une population nombreuse et diverse. Né le 27 octobre 1945 à Garanhuns, dans l’État du Pernambouc, Lula a connu un parcours exceptionnel : ouvrier métallurgiste, dirigeant syndical, fondateur du Parti des travailleurs, président de la République de 2003 à 2010, puis de nouveau élu en 2022 et réélu en 2026. Sa victoire à la veille de ses 81 ans constitue un symbole politique fort. Elle illustre sa longévité dans la vie publique brésilienne et sa capacité à conserver une base électorale suffisamment large pour remporter une compétition nationale particulièrement disputée. Mais le défi qui s’ouvre devant lui sera différent de celui de la campagne. Il lui faudra transformer cette victoire en capacité de gouverner, renouer le dialogue dans une société divisée et répondre aux attentes d’électeurs dont les priorités ne sont pas toujours les mêmes. Au-delà du résultat, la leçon de cette élection est claire : dans une démocratie polarisée, une avance au premier tour ou dans les sondages ne suffit pas à garantir la victoire finale. La participation électorale, la mobilisation des abstentionnistes, la qualité de la campagne et la capacité à élargir sa base peuvent modifier le cours d’un scrutin jusqu’au dernier moment. À la veille de ses 81 ans, Lula ne signe donc pas seulement un retour victorieux. Il entre dans l’histoire électorale brésilienne en devenant le premier candidat depuis le rétablissement du suffrage présidentiel direct à remporter le second tour après avoir terminé en deuxième position au premier. items.title: Cameroun : l’audition du lieutenant-colonel Ayissi Nanga attendue au tribunal militaire de Yaoundé
items.description: © DR La reprise ce 26 octobre du procès relatif à l’assassinat de Martinez Zogo questionne sur l’audition du lieutenant-colonel Parfait Arnaud Ayissi Nanga qui souhaite témoigner sur l’affaire dans laquelle il a travaillé au début des enquêtes. L’un des moments importants attendus au procès de Martinez Zogo qui reprend ce lundi 26 octobre est l’audition du lieutenant-colonel parfait Arnaud Ayissi Nanga. L’officier a interpellé sa hiérarchie militaire il y a quelque temps et a souhaité livrer son témoignage au tribunal militaire sur l’affaire. Indiquant être victime des menaces de mort depuis qu’il a exprimé sa volonté de témoigner, il a demandé la protection du tribunal. Suite à ses différentes sorties, il a été interpellé le 17 octobre, conduit au Secrétariat d’Etat à la défense chargé de la gendarmerie puis remis en liberté le lendemain. Peu avant, le 13 octobre, il s’est présenté aux juges du tribunal militaire alors que l’audition d’un autre témoin était encore en cours. Le président du tribunal avait donné instruction au commissaire du gouvernement de prendre des dispositions pouvant assurer sa sécurité. Au cours de cette phase du procès qui commence ce lundi, il est attendu qu’il se présente dans le box des témoins pour donner sa version des faits. Mais, son passage se fera au terme du contre-interrogatoire du lieutenant-colonel Dieudonné Bialo, 35è témoin de l’accusation. Dans cette contre-interrogation, il sera face à maxime Eko Eko, ancien patron de la direction générale de la recherche extérieure, accusé dans cette affaire. La suite du procès se fera avec d’éventuelles questions des parties au témoin et l’éventuel interrogatoire du ministère public. Le lieutenant-colonel Parfait Ayissi Nanga est compté parmi les responsables qui ont participé aux premières enquêtes sur l’assassinat de martinez Zogo. L’ancien commandant du groupement de gendarmerie du Mfoundi avait aussi intégré la commission mixte d’enquête gendarmerie et police formée à la demande du président de la République. Sa déposition pourrait révéler des détails sur la procédure au moment où il était impliqué dans l’enquête. Cet article Cameroun : l’audition du lieutenant-colonel Ayissi Nanga attendue au tribunal militaire de Yaoundé est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .

items.title: Phone-tapping charge: Court rejects El-Rufai’s no-case submission
items.description: …orders him to open his defence By Ikechukwu Nnochiri The Federal High Court in Abuja on Monday held that the detained former Kaduna State governor, Nasir El-Rufai, has a case to answer over an allegation that he unlawfully intercepted the phone communications of the National Security Adviser (NSA), Nuhu Ribadu. The court, in a ruling delivered by Justice Joyce Abdulmalik, dismissed as lacking in merit a no-case submission that the embattled former governor filed to be discharged and acquitted of the charge against him. El-Rufai, who was governor between 2015 and 2023 and also served as Minister of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT) under former President Olusegun Obasanjo’s administration, is facing trial over comments he made when he appeared as a guest on Arise Television on February 13. He is answering to a five-count amended charge that the Federal Government preferred against him through the Department of State Services (DSS). It was alleged that the defendant, during his appearance on Arise TV’s Prime Time programme in Abuja, admitted that he knew and was associated with an individual who had illegally intercepted the NSA’s telephone communications. Aside from the allegation that his action breached national security and public safety, an offence punishable under Section 12(1) of the Cybercrimes (Prohibition, Prevention, etc.) (Amendment) Act, 2024, the former governor was also charged with failing to report the crime to the relevant security agencies. The defendant had, during the TV interview, reacted to what he described as an attempt by DSS operatives to “abduct” him at Nnamdi Azikiwe International Airport in Abuja on February 12, 2026, upon his return from Cairo. He insisted that the security agency was being instigated by the ICPC, which he said had received a directive from the NSA, Ribadu, to detain him. The former governor claimed the information reached him through someone who had listened in on the NSA’s telephone conversations. Meanwhile, after the prosecution closed its case with the evidence of two witnesses who testified before the court, the defendant applied to be discharged and acquitted. El-Rufai, through his team of lawyers led by Mr. Paul Erokoro, SAN, insisted that the prosecution had failed to establish a prima facie case to warrant the court compelling him to enter a defence to the charge, which he described as incompetent. However, the prosecution counsel, Mr. Oluwole Aladedoye, SAN, urged the court to dismiss the application and order the defendant to open his defence to the charge. Aladedoye, SAN, maintained that the oral and documentary evidence laid before the court was sufficient to tie the defendant to the allegations against him. In her ruling on the matter, Justice Abdulmalik said the court was satisfied that the evidence laid by the prosecution was strong enough to warrant explanations from the defendant. Even though the court had yet to ascertain the defendant’s culpability or otherwise, it dismissed the no-case submission and ordered him to open his defence to the charge. It will be recalled that shortly after being accused of admitting that he used “technical equipment” to illegally intercept the NSA’s calls, El-Rufai filed a motion to stop his trial. He gave 17 reasons why the charge, marked FHC/ABJ/CR/99/2026, should be quashed by the court. He argued that the charge was incompetent and legally defective, insisting that the DSS had no legal basis to elevate a “casual remark” he made during a television interview into “a confession” that he had indeed tapped the NSA’s telephone line, as alleged. He argued that the statement he made on Arise TV did not constitute a confessional statement in law, saying that for a statement to be admissible as a confession, it must be made under caution, voluntarily, and in circumstances that satisfy the Judges’ Rules. El-Rufai maintained that the statements he made during his television interview were made without caution or warning, in a voluntary public discussion, and without the protections afforded to suspects in custody. “A casual remark on a television programme cannot be elevated to a judicial confession,” he further argued. However, the court declined to quash the charge and ordered an accelerated hearing of the case. El-Rufai who has been in detention since February is standing trial before courts in both Abuja and Kaduna state. Justice Abdulmalik had, on July 23, dismissed as lacking in merit an application that the former governor filed for the variation of his bail conditions, which he described as very stringent and difficult to fulfil. According to El-Rufai’s lawyer, the bail conditions sought to be varied included the requirement that the defendant produce level 17 civil servants with properties in Maitama or Asokoro, as well as verification and attestation letters from the Kaduna State traditional council. However, the prosecution opposed the variation request, insisting that qualified public officers who could meet the conditions existed and could easily be secured by the defendant. It persuaded the court to reject the application. The post Phone-tapping charge: Court rejects El-Rufai’s no-case submission appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Bouré Kouroulamini (Didi) : Finabala bientôt doté d’un poste de santé grâce aux fonds propres de la commune
items.description: L’équipe communale de Didi, dirigée par le maire, Mamadi Fanta Camara, a procédé au lancement des travaux de construction d’un poste de santé comprenant huit (8) salles, ainsi que d’un bloc de latrines à Bouré Finabala, dans le secteur du district de Nafadji. Si cet acte fondateur du développement est salué par les populations, la couverture médiatique de l’événement a cependant mis en lumière de graves dysfonctionnements organisationnels et une confusion des genres préoccupante entre communication de terrain et journalisme professionnel. C’est une véritable fête villageoise qui a accueilli la délégation communale à Bouré Finabala, un secteur stratégique du district de Nafadji. Hommes, femmes, sages et enfants : toutes les couches de la population se sont fortement mobilisées pour assister au lancement de ce chantier très attendu. Pour les villageois, cette initiative représente un immense soulagement et une avancée majeure vers l’amélioration de leurs conditions sanitaires. Ce projet de développement, le tout premier mené par la nouvelle équipe communale de la sous-préfecture de Kouroulamini (Didi), comprend : Un poste de santé doté de huit (8) salles de soins et de consultation ; Un bloc de latrines comprenant quatre (4) cabines répondant aux normes d’hygiène ; Un financement intégralement assuré par les fonds propres de la commune. Interrogé autour d’un plat d’honneur, le maire de la commune de Didi a exhorté les chefs locaux et l’ensemble de la population de Finabala à privilégier une cohabitation modérée et pacifique avec l’entreprise chargée des travaux. « accepter d'être toujours des bons voisins avec les travailleurs, suivre les opérations des travaux afin que le délais de 4 mois prévu dans le cahier de charge soit rigoureusement respecté. Ce n'est que le debut des grands projets que nous sommes entrain d'envisager pour Kouroulamini. » Sur le terrain, la portée républicaine de l’événement a malheureusement été ternie par une désorganisation totale. Aucun protocole officiel n’a été respecté : absence de présentations, aucune allocution formelle structurée et séances d’interviews organisées dans la plus grande confusion. Cette situation de désordre organisationnel serait la conséquence directe de l’omniprésence de personnes présentées comme de faux communicants, qui auraient exercé un monopole autour du maire et de sa délégation. Ce climat d’anarchie a empêché, d’une part, les journalistes professionnels d’exercer leur métier de manière rigoureuse. Parmi ces acteurs, un individu se présentant comme correspondant de la radio rurale de Siguiri s’est particulièrement illustré par un manque flagrant d’expérience, de déontologie et de professionnalisme, désorganisant ainsi l’ensemble de la couverture médiatique. Ce qui s’est passé à Bouré Finabala illustre une tendance inquiétante : une mutation de la fonction traditionnelle de griot vers un simulacre de journalisme. Ce glissement, souvent assimilé à de l’arnaque professionnelle, fragilise l’accès à une information de qualité. La réduction de l’espace accordé aux médias lors de cet événement semble découler d’une méconnaissance profonde des règles de la communication publique et du fonctionnement des médias par l’équipe communale actuelle. Pour que les actions de développement de la commune de Didi soient valorisées à leur juste valeur, il devient urgent que l’autorité communale apprenne à distinguer les animateurs de la foule des professionnels de l’information. Mamoudou Kéïta, correspondant basé à Kintinian 628 61 88 90 L’article Bouré Kouroulamini (Didi) : Finabala bientôt doté d’un poste de santé grâce aux fonds propres de la commune est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: Pakistan condemns Houthi attacks targeting Makkah, Madina as 'grave violation' of Saudi sovereignty
items.description: Pakistan on Monday condemned Houthi missile attacks targeting Saudi Arabia’s Makkah and Madina regions, terming them a “grave violation” of the kingdom’s sovereignty and territorial integrity. According to a statement issued by the Foreign Office (FO), these “reprehensible attacks constitute a grave violation of Saudi Arabia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity and demonstrate a blatant disregard for the sanctity of Islam’s holiest sites and the safety of civilians”. Pakistan reiterated its “unwavering solidarity” with Saudi Arabia and its firm commitment to the Makkah Alliance , the FO said. It reaffirmed its steadfast support for the kingdom’s security, stability and defence, including the protection of the Two Holy Mosques against any external aggression or threat. Pakistan also commended the “vigilance and efficiency” of Saudi air defence forces in countering the attacks, it said. A day earlier, the Muslim World League also condemned Houthi attacks targeting Makkah and Madina. In a statement, the Makkah-based organisation said the attacks showed “disregard for the danger of frightening the feelings of more than two billion Muslims, and the violation of the values of our true religion, and the most basic principles of humanity”. The condemnations came after the Houthis said they had launched attacks on Saudi oil facilities and airports on Saturday, prompting the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Yemen rebel group to announce that it had intercepted two ballistic missiles as clashes between the sides intensified. Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group had targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, an Aramco facility in Yanbu, the Rabigh oil refinery, crude oil pumping stations and the East-West Pipeline. He also said the group had targeted King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, an airport in Najran and an airbase in Khamis Mushait. The Saudi-led coalition said it had destroyed two ballistic missiles fired towards Yanbu and Taif. Saudi Civil Defence said debris from intercepted missiles had fallen in the Makkah and Madina regions. It said fragments of intercepted missiles had fallen in Wadi al-Mughammas in Makkah, as well as in areas of Jeddah, Taif and Rabigh. The Houthis subsequently denied targeting Makkah and Madina, saying their operations were directed at “Saudi oil facilities and military bases”. The renewed fighting has shattered a UN-brokered truce reached in 2022 that largely halted cross-border attacks between the Saudi-led coalition, which backs Yemen’s internationally recognised government, and the Houthis, who control the capital, Sanaa.

items.title: Broken record: A 'holocaust' in East Punjab, literacy rates and the Palestine question
items.description: Two weeks after independence, communal violence, particularly in East Punjab, dominated the headlines, with the Quaid-i-Azam having to make a fervent appeal for peace. In other major developments between Aug 25 and 31, 1947, Madar-i-Millat Ms Fatima Jinnah reiterated the need for women’s literacy, Pakistan opened its first embassy in Washington DC, while different solutions to the Palestine question were discussed in the United Nations. In the Aug 25 issue, the headline of the main story on page one quoted the Quaid urging his countrymen to “Preserve peace for [the] sake of Pakistan’.” “Those who think they can undo Pakistan are sadly mistaken,” Mr Jinnah observed. He was referring to communal violence in East Punjab. “I have been watching with increasing grief and concern the orgies of violence in the Eastern Punjab which have taken … a heavy toll on Muslim lives.” In fact, in the Aug 27 issue, the lead story, describing the situation as a “continued holocaust in the East Punjab,” said that the violence in that Indian state had resulted in over a quarter million refugees. “Ferozepur, Hoshiarpur, Jullundur, Gurdaspur, Ludhiana and Ambala are still hotbeds of massacre and other brutalities,” the report added grimly. The Quaid reminded his countrymen to be wary and prevent communal disturbances in Pakistan: “It is of the utmost importance that Pakistan should be kept absolutely free from disorder. …” Mr Jinnah had good reason to be worried, for in the weeks after independence, Lahore and other parts of Punjab had witnessed communal killings, while in the Aug 25 edition, a report mentioned that Sardar Abdur Rab Nishtar, the Communication Minister, had to be dispatched to Balochistan to quell disturbances there. Unlike the present, the violence at the time was of a religious nature. “The situation is absolutely normal”, Sardar Nishtar claimed after a visit to Quetta. “I toured the area that was burnt and also Hindu and Sikh areas. I also went to the refugee camps and inspected arrangements for their accommodation and rations. … I feel that now by the grace of God, the situation is absolutely normal. …” Women’s literacy drive Also in the Aug 25 edition, Ms Fatima Jinnah hinted at the launch of a literacy drive for women. “Education,” the Quaid’s sister said, “was the pre-requisite for the advancement of any nation … at the earliest opportunity a big drive will be launched to stamp out illiteracy from amongst the women of Pakistan. …” These were of course progressive, noble thoughts. Some estimates indicate female literacy was under 10 per cent in Pakistan at the time of Independence, while being virtually zero in rural parts of the country. It would be wrong to say no progress has been made, as today female literacy stands at around 54pc. But have we done enough? Unfortunately, successive rulers failed to replicate the zeal Pakistan’s founders had for spreading literacy, even though several ‘education emergencies’ have been declared. The results of officialdom’s neglect over the decades? At least 25-26 million children of school age remain out of school today, while tens of millions of adult Pakistanis cannot read or write. One wonders what the founders of this nation would make of these abysmal figures. Good morning America The relationship between Pakistan and the United States has been a tumultuous one, with the former once being considered Uncle Sam’s ‘most allied ally’ in this region, helping fight an American anti-Soviet ‘jihad’ in Afghanistan, and experiencing numerous other ups and downs. That relationship, as documented in Dawn ’s Aug 26 issue, in a sense formally began on Aug 25, 1947, when the Pakistan Embassy opened its temporary quarters in Washington DC. “The Pakistan Embassy opened for normal business at the temporary headquarters at the Choreham Hotel today with Charge d’Affaires, Mr M.O. Baig declaring: “We are truly operating.” Our man in DC was scouting for a permanent embassy site in “overcrowded Washington” while observing that “My country is beginning from scratch in its relations with foreign countries. Therefore, there are various basic agreements that will have to be negotiated. …” Of course, the Pakistani mission in DC would later move to other buildings, but this long, complicated relationship began from a temporary abode in a Washington hotel. Palestine solution The Palestine question has remained unresolved for nearly eight decades, and at the time of Pakistan’s birth — Israel had not yet come into existence and the British were in charge of Mandatory Palestine — several solutions were being debated in the UN. According to a report in the Aug 28 edition, several proposals were discussed at the UNO (as it was then known) Special Committee Meeting in Geneva. According to one plan, the federal solution would result in the creation of six “cantons” in Palestine, “three Jewish and three Arab, having a Central Government on lines similar to that of Switzerland.” The other idea was for semi-independent Jewish and Arab states. Of course, none of these ideas would come to fruition, and the following year (1948) would witness the acceleration of the Nakba and the creation of Israel. As for the people of Palestine, they still await justice, and the right to live as free human beings on their own land. With the advantage of hindsight, one has the opportunity to study the historical cycles in a nation’s life. Thanks to this newspaper’s unique, extensive archive of back issues, one can examine the major political, economic and social trends that have shaped Pakistan and the world over the last seven decades and counting. Cliched as it may sound, history repeats itself, and we — as a state and as a polity — largely refuse to learn from it. Through this platform, we will look back at the ‘big’ stories that made it to the front pages of Dawn, as well as significant developments tucked away in the inside pages, from the birth of Pakistan onwards, and try to put them in perspective. We will study the critical issues of the week, starting from Aug 14, 1947 and examine the major themes and issues that made it to the paper.

items.title: Pétrochimie : 4 groupes étrangers présélectionnés pour réaliser deux usines en Algérie
items.description: Les deux pôles de l’industrie pétrochimique algérienne seront renforcés par de nouvelles capacités : une unité de production d’huiles de base à Arzew et un complexe de production d'éthylène à Skikda. Des entreprises internationales ont été présélectionnées par Sonatrach pour la conception et la gestion des deux projets. Une unité d’huile à Arzew et un complexe d’éthylène à Skikda L’information a été rapportée par le média MEED (Middle East Economic Digest). Selon la même source, la présélection a débuté en août 2025 et la date limite de soumission des offres a été prolongée. Pour le moment, quatre entreprises sont retenues. Il s'agit de China HuanQiu Contracting & Engineering (Chine), Enppi (Égypte), Técnicas Reunidas (Espagne) et Wood, un groupement émirati-britannique. Les prestations attendues portent sur l'ingénierie et la conception préliminaires, l'acquisition des licences de procédés et les services de conseil en gestion de projet, a indiqué MEED. Selon les explications fournies, l'unité prévue à Arzew produira des huiles de base des groupes II et III. Il s’agit de produits pétroliers hautement raffinés utilisés dans la fabrication d'huiles moteur, de lubrifiants industriels et de lubrifiants spéciaux. L'éthylène que produira le complexe de Skikda est “ une matière première pétrochimique majeure ”, destinée essentiellement à la fabrication du polyéthylène, le plastique le plus produit au monde, explique-t-on. Algérie : porter la part des hydrocarbures transformés de 32 à 50 % Les deux unités entrent dans le cadre de la stratégie de l'Algérie qui tend à développer le raffinage, la pétrochimie et la transformation en aval “afin de traiter davantage d'hydrocarbures sur son territoire au lieu d'exporter du pétrole brut, du gaz ou des produits intermédiaires à faible valeur ajoutée ”, a indiqué le média moyen-oriental. Celui-ci rappelle qu'en juin 2025, le ministre des Hydrocarbures Mohamed Arkab a fixé l’objectif de faire passer de 32 % à 50 % sur cinq ans la part des hydrocarbures transformés en produits à plus forte valeur ajoutée. Des investissements de 7 milliards de dollars ont été annoncés à cet effet. En mars 2024 Sonatrach a attribué à l’Italien Tecnimont un contrat de 1,1 milliard de dollars pour la réalisation à Skikda d’une usine d'alkylbenzène linéaire d’une capacité de 100 000 tonnes par an. L’article Pétrochimie : 4 groupes étrangers présélectionnés pour réaliser deux usines en Algérie est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: Du village d’enfants SOS de Louga aux réseaux sociaux : le parcours inspirant des frères Koué
items.description: Des traits de caractère similaires, un timbre de voix presque identique. Et non, ce n'est pas le fruit du hasard. La ressemblance est frappante : ce ne sont pas de simples sosies, mais bien des frères jumeaux. Eux, ce sont Brice et Serge Koué. Âgés de plus de 35 ans, nés et ayant grandi au Sénégal, ces deux frères dynamiques de nationalité sénégalo-ivoirienne incarnent un parcours aussi passionnant que résilient. Un petit indice pour les distinguer aujourd'hui ? La coiffure et le style. Serge porte des locks, tandis que Brice arbore une coupe afro. Au-delà des apparences, leurs personnalités s'affirment différemment : Serge est souvent perçu comme le plus extraverti et « social » des deux, ce que confirme son frère jumeau : « Sur le plan comportemental, Serge est plus “social”, on aurait dit “plus gentil” », tandis que Brice brille par sa plume et sa rhétorique. Surnommé le « Senghor des temps modernes » par ses nombreux abonnés, Brice ne doit pas ce titre uniquement à son esthétique. Habile orateur, responsable des relations publiques de formation en RH et finances, il maîtrise le verbe et manie la langue de Molière avec la précision d'un poète. Serge, quant à lui, a fait ses armes en informatique, un domaine dans lequel il met aujourd'hui ses compétences au service de Médecins Sans Frontières. Mais avant le monde virtuel, le destin des jumeaux s'est forgé dans le cadre bien particulier du Village d'Enfants SOS de Louga. C'est là qu'ils ont passé toute leur enfance et le début de leur adolescence, une expérience fondatrice qui a forgé leur courage, leur force et un amour inconditionnel pour le service à l'humain. Fidèles à la culture du give back (NDLR : « redonner » en français est un principe philosophique et managérial qui consiste à partager son succès, son temps ou ses ressources avec sa communauté ou la société, en signe de gratitude pour les opportunités reçues), ils continuent de soutenir leur communauté à leur manière. « Pour du give back, Brice a écrit un livre intitulé « Souvenirs et perspectives », destiné aux enfants qui ont grandi là-bas avec nous et aux autres qui nous ont succédé. » Serge a travaillé pour l’institution pendant près d’une décennie. « Lorsque nous le pouvons, nous faisons un geste de solidarité, mais il faut dire que nous ne sommes plus très présents aux côtés des villages SOS maintenant », reconnaît Brice. Éclairer les esprits Très actifs sur Internet, Brice et Serge ne publient pas pour ne rien dire. De 2016 à 2023, ils ont animé « La chronique des jumeaux », un espace d'engagement citoyen et d'analyse politique. Après avoir mis en pause cette activité en 2024 pour se recentrer sur leur vie personnelle, ils ont relancé leur dynamique sous le concept « T-Twin Talk » (un clin d'œil entre Twin talk et To win talk, la « discussion pour gagner ») : « C’est un concept assez facile où mon frère et moi traitons de sujets très accessibles et donnons nos avis dans le respect. Ce sont des vidéos qu’on veut courtes (max. 2 min), mais qu’on espère utiles au public qui nous suit et semble bien apprécier », d’après Serge. À travers ce nouveau projet, les jumeaux décortiquent des mots français à connotation positive pour inspirer leur communauté à surmonter les difficultés du quotidien. Dès que les caméras s'allument, les deux frères s'engagent dans une véritable transmission où se mêlent sagesse, maturité, légèreté et connaissance. Sans jamais impacter négativement leur vie professionnelle, les réseaux sociaux sont devenus pour eux un terrain d'expression naturelle : un espace où se croisent le rire, la réflexion et l'envie profonde d'éclairer les esprits. En transformant leur vécu en force et le verbe en outil d'éveil, Brice et Serge Koué prouvent qu'au-delà de la ressemblance physique, c'est un même idéal qui les unit : celui d'éclairer les esprits, un mot à la fois. Fatou NGOM

items.title: Losing the ‘Big-Ass Truck’ Vote
items.description: Photographs by Brian Finke for The Atlantic A long the highways and farm road s of the southern tip of Texas, the bright-red campaign signs for Eric Flores are impossible to miss. Flores, the Republican candidate for the state’s Thirty-Fourth Congressional District, has Ken-doll looks, with gel-stiff hair and the kind of physique that Donald Trump admires. His bio appears across the top of the sign: Infantry Officer. Prosecutor. Father. A second set of nearly identical red signs are scattered across the district, only these show Flores with President Trump giving a thumbs-up, sandwiched between the declarations Trump Endorsed and Support ICE! When I first saw these signs, I did a double take. Why would any candidate want to be associated with ICE in the Rio Grande Valley, where the population is more than 90 percent Hispanic? The answer appeared in tiny letters at the bottom: Paid for by Northern Cameron County Democrats. The attack ad captures how much has changed since Trump won in the Rio Grande Valley two years ago. Hispanic voters—especially men—were a key part of the national coalition that put Trump back in the White House. Trump and Joe Biden roughly split the votes of Latinos in 2024, after several cycles of Democratic presidential candidates winning the group by double digits. Exit polls in Texas estimated that Trump won Hispanic voters there by 10 percentage points. But that support appears to have evaporated. Nationally, nearly one-fifth of Latinos who voted for Trump in 2024 now say they do not want Republicans to control Congress, a poll earlier this month found. And a late-summer survey of Hispanic Texans who are likely to vote in the upcoming election showed Democrats with a 2-to-1 advantage. The Rio Grande Valley had been a Democratic stronghold for decades, and the region is crucial to the party’s midterm-elections strategy. The Texas U.S. Senate race has become the nation’s most expensive contest of 2026, as James Talarico tries to become the first Democrat to win statewide office there in more than 30 years. Recent polls show him in a dead heat with Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton. For Talarico to win, Democrats need the Rio Grande Valley to swing back, which would make Trump’s 2024 multiracial MAGA coalition look more like a one-off. For Republicans, a Talarico win would be a political and psychological blow, signaling a new purple era for the state made possible by a population that’s trending more urban and college educated, and less white. GOP candidates, taking their cues from the president, have been framing the election in apocalyptic terms, telling voters that a Republican loss will usher in communism, open borders, and gender anarchy. Paxton frequently says: “If we lose Texas, we lose America.” Elon Musk donated $158 million last month to the main super PAC supporting Senate Republicans to flood the airwaves with negative ads. [ Read: ‘We have not seen ugly yet’ ] I spent several days earlier this month driving around the Rio Grande Valley to speak with voters and candidates. I found a fair amount of sympathy for Trump among those who voted for him two years ago. Negative ads and wild social-media claims left others unsure whom to believe. It was clear to me that the region’s political realignment remains in flux. Hispanics in South Texas, especially men, remain up for grabs in a way they weren’t before Trump came along. Brian Finke R epresentative Vicente Gonzalez , the Democratic incumbent running against Flores, barely held his seat in 2024, winning by less than 3 percentage points. Since then, Republicans have recast the district’s boundaries, pushing farther north into the more conservative-leaning Corpus Christi. Gonzalez, a former trial attorney who was first elected in 2016, is running as a folksy, I-feel-your-pain populist, not a tough guy, with ads that flip between Spanish and English. One shows Gonzalez grilling steaks at a backyard cookout and rationing meager portions to disappointed guests as he blames Trump’s tariffs for high food prices. I had lunch with Gonzalez and about 20 of his supporters earlier this month at Frijoles, a restaurant in Brownsville. The group was mostly men, a mix of taxi drivers and local business owners who cracked jokes about involuntarily losing weight from smaller hamburgers. Steve Torres, who operates 11 Airbnbs that house engineers working at Musk’s nearby Starbase, told Gonzalez that his electricity bills are soaring. “I’m paying more than $4,000 a month,” said Torres, who voted for Trump. Last year, he closed two restaurants that he owned after struggling to compete with franchises that could better withstand higher costs. Gonzalez told the group that 200 fishing boats are moored along the Gulf Coast in the district because owners can’t turn a profit with diesel at $6 a gallon. Others at the table grumbled about labor shortages created by Trump’s immigration crackdown. Workers are scared to leave their homes, and ICE sightings—real and imagined—are shared widely on social media. Gonzalez said he knows a restaurant owner who had to close one of his three locations because he didn’t have staff. “I know a farmer with 15,000 acres who only planted half because he doesn’t have enough workers for the harvest,” Gonzalez told the group. Chuck Rocha, a political consultant who is advising Democrats in the state, told me that lots of voter groups are moving away from Trump, but that Latino men appear to be doing so at a larger rate “because they were some of the biggest swingers to Trump over the past 10 years.” Rocha has helped Democratic candidates create messages appealing to what he calls “the big-ass-truck economy for Latino men.” Those voters want to provide for their families and enjoy the money they earn, Rocha said. “When I was making a TV ad a couple of weeks ago, a guy pointed to his truck in the front yard and said, That fucking thing has become a lawn ornament because I can't afford to drive it ,” Rocha said. [ Read: Going hungry in Trump’s economy ] Republicans have been using their fundraising edge to saturate South Texas with ads aimed at the region’s social conservatism. The Flores campaign has put up signs claiming that Gonzalez wants taxpayer-funded “child sex changes” because he voted against Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act last summer. His attorney sent the billboard company a cease-and-desist letter demanding removal of the advertisements showing Flores with Trump, The Washington Sun reported . Brian Finke Representative Vicente Gonzalez shakes hands at Luby’s at Sunrise Mall in Brownsville, Texas. One evening, I walked around a rough-looking colonia knocking on doors with Roel Garza, a 20-year-old business student canvassing for Democrats. Roosters erupted in several yards, and a guy in a welding mask was fixing a cattle trailer with a blowtorch, shooting sparks out of his carport. We sought out residents on Garza’s list who’d voted in previous cycles, avoiding the homes with barking dogs. One man who smelled of alcohol and had bloodshot eyes came out of his trailer to fire up a charcoal grill, and told us he’d voted for Trump but didn’t realize another election was coming up. Rosalina Saenz, a mother of six, told us she voted for Trump last time and was still happy with him. She told Garza that she was open to voting for Democrats in local races, but wasn’t sure who to support, because she’d seen so many ads “trashing” the candidates. Garza told me that he thought a lot of people backed Trump last time because “they wanted that macho figure.” But they remain open to persuasion. It was just a matter of getting them to connect the administration’s policies with the problems in their lives. “Once people know the issues, they’re smart enough to know how they want to vote,” Garza said. T he home-building industry in South Texas is where Trump’s least popular actions have converged to squeeze men working in construction. High mortgage rates have sapped housing demand, fuel prices are driving up construction costs, and the ICE crackdown has squeezed the labor supply. Benny Melendez, a general contractor who started his business seven years ago, invited me to a half-built house he is trying to finish outside McAllen. Melendez told me that he used to build on spec, investing his own money in a project with confidence that he’d quickly flip a sale. Now he builds only for clients who pay up front. Building a house used to take him four months, but now it takes eight to 12, he said, because he can’t find enough workers. Melendez voted for Trump two years ago and doesn’t “hate” him. He was less generous, and more profane, about the Trump adviser Stephen Miller, who orchestrated an ICE crackdown that has become so disruptive that Melendez and other members of his trade group felt like they had to get more involved in politics. At least 15 men he used to work with have been deported, and several of them were arrested by ICE en route to a job site. “If you have a ladder on your truck, they’ll start following you, and they’ll stop you,” Melendez said. “It is difficult for me to hear a 40-, 50-year-old guy cry in private with me, telling me he’s afraid that ICE is going to take him.” Melendez told me that the Rio Grande Valley is best-known for having a low cost of living and being family-oriented. “And now those are the two things being taken away from us,” he said. Brian Finke Benny Melendez, a general contractor who voted for Trump, visits a house he is building. Brian Finke A crew of subcontractors working for Melendez was supposed to install kitchen cabinets at the house that day. They didn’t show. Neither did the guys scheduled to pave the driveway. ICE vehicles had been spotted that morning in the area, and alerts had gone out across radio stations and social media. Most of the ICE officers making the arrests are other Hispanic men who grew up in the Rio Grande Valley, Melendez said, and as he watched video clips from construction sites, he recognized a close friend, despite his face mask. “I wrote to my friend and said, Dude, you know I love you, but you’re losing my respect ,” he said. Melendez was even more disgusted when the friend told him the pay was too good to quit. Melendez told me that construction workers across the Rio Grande Valley tune in each morning to the radio show El Zorro y Su Pandilla (“The Fox and His Gang”), which relays reports of ICE sightings. I went to see “El Zorro,” whose real name is Hector Lepe, at his home studio in Donna, where a pickup truck parked in the driveway was plastered with a promotional picture of Lepe and his wife. Lepe told me that callers often dial in to his show describing encounters with ICE and fears of what will happen to their families if they’re deported. It’s made him something of a community therapist for men who don’t have the time or money to see a professional. Lepe, who grew up in Oaxaca, in southern Mexico, said he crossed the border illegally as a young man and spent years as an itinerant farmworker until he broke into broadcasting. He obtained legal status through his marriage and became a U.S. citizen. Even though the Rio Grande Valley is a border community, and has federal immigration officers and agents everywhere, it used to be a “place where you could take your family to the movies, to the circus, to eat, to dance” without fear. Lepe said that he’s been especially bothered by stories of recently deported tradesmen being reduced to working in low-wage Mexican assembly plants along the border. They’ve been separated from their children in the United States but try to remain as physically close as possible. “Imagine one day you get up to go to work, and they just take you,” Lepe said. He told me that he plans to launch a new project, La Rescata (“The Rescue”), for men in ICE custody to call so that someone will secure their truck and tools until a family member can safely retrieve them. He’s been encouraging listeners to register to vote if they’re eligible, and to show up for Democrats. F lat and muggy , the Lower Rio Grande Valley is about 250 miles south of San Antonio, and for most of the past century, it was practically an island, with Mexico on one side and millions of acres of Texas cattle ranches and scrublands on the other. Its counties have some of the highest poverty rates in Texas. Their residents were reliable Democratic voters who benefitted from the social-welfare policies of the New Deal and President Lyndon B. Johnson’s Great Society. The RGV was LBJ country. The North American Free Trade Agreement of 1994 transformed the Rio Grande Valley into a trade and logistics hub for the manufacturing boom in northern Mexico. Its population doubled to about 1.5 million, and today the McAllen metropolitan area is the state’s fifth largest after Dallas, Houston, San Antonio, and Austin. Wealthy and middle-class families from northern Mexico began arriving, too, fleeing drug-cartel violence and kidnapping-for-ransom terror. Developers gobbled up farmland to build subdivisions and faux-Mediterranean mansions not far from unincorporated colonias with dusty ranch houses and trailers. For working-class Hispanic families, the Rio Grande Valley offered a South Texas version of the American dream with big houses, cheap gas, and plentiful jobs. Bobby Pulido, the Democratic candidate in the Fifteenth Congressional District, has been campaigning on nostalgia for that aspirational vision. “The thing that the Democratic Party doesn’t understand is you don’t get anywhere down here calling people ‘the rich,’ as if it’s pejorative,” he told me. “That’s what a lot of people here aspire to be!” We were driving around a wealthy suburb in Edinburg, not far from where Pulido grew up. [ Read: The return of the Democratic manly man ] Pulido, who is 53, was already a celebrity in the Rio Grande Valley, a two-time Latin Grammy–winning Tejano-music star whose 1995 hit “ Desvelado ” (“Sleepless”) featured a video of him wandering San Francisco, singing of unrequited love. Pulido’s Republican opponent, Representative Monica De La Cruz, dismissed him early in the race as unqualified, a washed-up singer from quinceañera parties. The comment backfired when Pulido started playing for free at local quinceañeras, generating publicity and easy access to large gatherings of potential voters who, Pulido notes, are already celebrating and drinking when he arrives. Pulido’s family has long straddled music and politics. His father, Roberto, is a Tejano icon; his uncle was the top Hidalgo County executive and another uncle was its district attorney. Pulido studied political science in college, and—like Trump—is a natural showman, campaigning with swagger and a flair for spectacle. Last weekend, he played a concert to a sold-out arena. His opening act was a mariachi band that includes several members who were arrested this year by ICE. De La Cruz won the district in 2024 by more than 14 points, but the latest polls show Pulido ahead. His campaign has focused on high gas prices, tariffs, and ICE cases that have stirred local outrage. Pulido denounced the actions of ICE last month after officers pepper-sprayed and detained two 17-year-old U.S. citizens, and this month he called attention to the government’s attempt to deport Giovanna Perez , a mother of four whose husband was at Army basic training when she tried to pick up her family’s military-ID cards at a base in Corpus Christi and was turned over to ICE. Bobby Pulido attends a political rally. I asked Pulido about the shifting politics of immigration enforcement in the Rio Grande Valley, where jobs at Border Patrol and other federal law-enforcement agencies have long been a path to middle-class life, especially for many Hispanic men whose parents immigrated here. Trump’s inroads with Hispanic voters two years ago were partly fueled by frustration with Biden’s inability to contain mass migration, as hundreds of thousands of migrants and asylum seekers—mostly from Central and South America—streamed into the region, overwhelming local charities and public services. “When I was growing up, we were all Tejanos here for the most part. There were not many Mexicans,” Pulido told me. “This was a pass-through area, where people would go up north to look for opportunity.” That changed when drug-war violence sent families fleeing for safety. “Our restaurants got a lot better, because they started bringing in Mexican cuisine. Then, slowly but surely, they brought businesses, they started investing, and, man, we started booming. We started growing, and then something else happened: We started integrating with them,” he said. The next day, I went to a happy-hour event for De La Cruz at a nearby tavern. There were about 40 people in the room, and De La Cruz, a former insurance agent, told them she got into politics to stand up for Border Patrol agents after a neighbor, the wife of an agent, had asked for donations of stuffed animals to give to children coming across the border without their parents. “I wanted to be their voice. I wanted to stand up,” De La Cruz told the crowd. Like other Republican candidates, De La Cruz told her supporters that the implications of the midterms would extend far beyond South Texas. “This election is about making sure that your grandchildren, that your great-grandchildren, will have a free country to live in,” she said. The September 11, 2001, attacks were a galvanizing moment in her life, she noted, adding that Democrats had selected “a radical Islamic communist” as mayor of New York City “where the Twin Towers fell,” referring to Zohran Mamdani. The audience responded with cheers. “This election is about saving the soul of our country that was founded on Judeo-Christian values,” she shouted. More quietly, De La Cruz has tried to distance herself from Trump’s mass-deportation policies, and during an interview after her speech, she told me that she supports “common-sense enforcement policy.” I asked why she voted, along with other Republicans, for two bills that together gave ICE more than $100 billion for immigration enforcement—10 times its annual operation budget. De La Cruz tried to steer the conversation to affordability and grew irritated when I pressed her about the ICE funding. She said she is candid with Republican leaders in Washington and tells them that enforcement should focus on criminals, “not hardworking families,” and that when a constituent needs help with ICE, her support for the Department of Homeland Security gives her clout that Democrats lack. “When I call Washington, D.C., for one of these families, guess what? They pick up the phone,” she told me. Brian Finke [ Read: The Republicans are bolting from Trump ] Her campaign has been attacking Pulido for having played with a former bandmate who was a convicted sex offender. (Pulido says that he hadn’t been aware of the man’s criminal record and cut ties when he learned about the conviction.) Last week, De La Cruz seemed eager to distance herself further from the White House, and was running new ads that tout her as a corruption fighter who will stand up to members of her own party. T he next day , I went to see a Democratic candidate whose win seems like a foregone conclusion: Representative Henry Cuellar, an 11-time incumbent. Cuellar was meeting with supporters at a private residence where plates of cabrito (“kid goat”) were served around a pool. Trump had just called Cuellar a “LOSER,” and “one of the most disloyal political people on Earth!” in a Truth Social post. The president told Republicans to vote for Tano Tijerina, a former Democrat who switched parties in 2024. In 2024, Cuellar and his wife were indicted on more than a dozen counts of bribery and corruption-related charges for allegedly taking $600,000 from an Azerbaijani energy company and a Mexican bank. Cuellar denied wrongdoing. Trump pardoned him last year, but to the president’s disappointment, Cuellar stayed with the Democratic Party. Republicans redrew the boundaries of Cuellar’s district last year, but they used Trump’s 2024 margin of victory, rather than the closer margins of local races, to calculate their advantage. As Hispanic voters have swung back toward the Democrats, Cuellar’s district has turned bluer. The latest polls show him with a double-digit lead, and earlier this month the largest Republican House PAC essentially raised a white flag, redirecting $3 million in planned spending to more competitive races. Cuellar’s district includes Starr County, one of the poorest in the state, which has a Hispanic population of about 97 percent. Trump lost to Hillary Clinton there by 60 points in 2016. Eight years later, Trump won it with almost 58 percent of the vote. It was the first time the county had voted for a Republican president since 1892. Cuellar told me that many of his constituents are men who work in oil and gas, and they once feared Kamala Harris would squeeze the industry. Now they’re getting crushed when they fill up their pickup trucks. “People used to tell me: El Trumpo va muy fuerte. Not anymore. The wind has changed. And the two issues are immigration and the cost of things,” Cuellar said, using the Spanish for “Trump is really strong.” Cuellar’s district includes the border town of Roma, whose historic downtown is perched on a bluff overlooking the Rio Grande. The Trump administration had installed a floating orange barrier in the middle of the channel to block migrants from swimming across. It looked like a giant pool noodle. Mass crossings into the Rio Grande Valley during Biden’s term galvanized voters for Trump in 2024. At the McAllen Country Club, I met with Judge Richard Cortez, the chief executive for Hidalgo County, who had to deal with the crisis. The golf course was under renovation, so the club looked out on a parched expanse of barren hills and construction machinery. Cortez was one of the South Texas Democrats who had urged the White House to halt illegal border crossings even if it meant angering pro-immigrant groups in the party’s base. “I knew Biden was in trouble with immigration because we were living it,” Cortez told me. He invited Biden to visit—twice, he said—to no avail. When I asked Cortez whether he thought Trump still retained support among male voters in the district, he introduced me to a group of men drinking whiskey and playing dominoes across the bar. Cortez said they were local big shots in real estate and manufacturing. All four men said they planned to vote Republican. “The Hispanic vote has gotten more conservative here,” one of the men, Henry Temkin, told me. “People are getting a little bit more knowledgeable. They’re not voting straight Democratic like they used to. They’re analyzing what the policies are.” He said he didn’t believe the polls showing Democrats poised to win. During my visit, I kept thinking back to something that Rocha, the political consultant, had told me: Many of these voters are not “voting for the Democrats because they love the Democrats.” The party has a lot of work to do before the 2028 presidential election, he said. Many Rio Grande Valley voters who supported Trump in 2024 still backed Democrat candidates in local races downballot. But the Democrats’ legacy advantage is fading in a place where families are acutely sensitive to big changes in federal policies—on immigration, taxes, inflation. Election support will be won and lost based on whether the government is making voters’ lives better, or not. Jack Rodriquez-Vars contributed research for this story.
